subtitle: ATR (Average True Range) measures recent volatility as a single number. Use it to size your stop loss to the asset's actual movement instead of a fixed %. Stops based on ATR scale automatically — no more tight stops on volatile coins and wide stops on calm ones.

blocks.content:
You learned position sizing in lesson 7: notional = $risk / SL distance %. The formula is correct but assumes you know the right SL distance. ATR gives you an objective, volatility-aware way to set that SL distance.

Without ATR, traders typically use fixed % stops ("always 2% below entry"). The problem: 2% on a calm BTC trade might be inside normal noise (you'll get stopped on routine fluctuation). 2% on a volatile alt might be inside a single candle's range (almost guaranteed stop-out). ATR solves this by sizing stops to RECENT ACTUAL volatility.

ATR (Average True Range) measures the AVERAGE RANGE of recent candles, accounting for gaps. Default period is 14 candles. The output is a price-denominated number — same units as the asset.

If 14-period ATR on BTC 4H is $1,200, that means the average true range over the last 14 four-hour candles was $1,200. Use this to scale your SL:

  • 1× ATR stop = $1,200 below entry (will get hit in normal volatility ~once every 2-4 candles)
  • 1.5× ATR stop = $1,800 below entry (typical conservative SL)
  • 2× ATR stop = $2,400 below entry (wide stop — hard to trigger from normal noise)
  • 3× ATR stop = $3,600 below entry (very wide — only triggered by major moves)
Why fixed % stops fail across assets

rows: Wide enough — most noise won't hit it
Inside normal noise — almost always stopped

blocks.content: The same 2% number is too tight on some assets and too wide on others. ATR adapts. "1.5× ATR" is approximately the same level of conservativeness across every asset because it scales with that asset's actual volatility.

blocks.title: The ATR rule of thumb
blocks.content:
For most active trading, set SL at 1.5× ATR below entry (for longs) or above entry (for shorts). This gives the trade room for normal volatility without being so wide that risk math becomes unworkable.

For very tight scalp setups, 0.75-1× ATR. For long-term swing trades, 2-3× ATR.
ATR + structural SL — best of both worlds

Pure ATR-based stops can occasionally place SL at meaningless levels (in the middle of nothing). Pure structural stops (below the last swing low) can be inappropriately tight on volatile days.

The hybrid approach:

  1. Identify the STRUCTURAL stop location — below the swing low, below the support level, below the engulfing candle's low.
  2. Check the ATR distance.
  3. If structural SL is closer than 0.75× ATR, widen it to 0.75-1× ATR (volatility room).
  4. If structural SL is further than 2× ATR, consider whether the trade is appropriate at current risk size.
  5. Otherwise, use the structural SL — it has both technical meaning AND adequate volatility room.
ATR for sizing — the integration with the position-size formula

Lesson 7 formula: notional = (equity × risk%) / SL distance %.

If you use ATR for SL distance:

  • Account: $10,000
  • Risk per trade: 1% = $100
  • BTC 4H ATR: $1,200, entry $60,000
  • SL at 1.5× ATR = $1,800 below entry = $58,200
  • SL distance % = $1,800 / $60,000 = 3.0%
  • Notional = $100 / 0.03 = $3,333

This scales perfectly. If ATR is bigger (volatile market), SL is wider, notional is smaller. Risk stays at 1%. The math protects you from oversizing in volatile periods without you having to manually adjust.

Same logic applies to TPs. If a trade has a 1.5× ATR stop, the TP needs to be at LEAST 1.5× ATR away to have a 1:1 risk:reward. Better:

  • TP1 = 2× ATR (1.33:1 R:R)
  • TP2 = 3× ATR (2:1 R:R)
  • TP3 = 4-5× ATR (2.67-3.33:1 R:R)

This ensures TPs are realistic given current volatility. In low-volatility markets, ATR-based TPs are appropriately conservative. In high-vol markets, TPs are appropriately ambitious.

blocks.title: ATR rising vs falling tells you regime
blocks.content:
ATR isn't static. Watch it over time:

  • ATR rising: volatility expanding. Markets are getting more active. Wider stops + bigger TPs needed. Trade smaller notional to keep dollar risk constant.
  • ATR falling: volatility contracting. Markets calming. Tighter stops possible. Often precedes a Bollinger Squeeze and eventual expansion.
  • ATR at historic lows: extreme calm. Almost always followed by expansion. Set up for breakout trades.

This makes ATR not just a sizing tool but a regime indicator — telling you when to expect expansion.

1. Using ATR alone for SL placement. Pure ATR stops can land at structurally meaningless levels. Better to combine with structural SLs.
  2. Ignoring ATR and using fixed %. The classic mistake. Same SL on different volatilities = different actual risk profiles.
  3. Using the wrong timeframe ATR. ATR is timeframe-specific. 1H ATR is much smaller than 4H ATR, which is smaller than daily. Match the ATR period to your trade timeframe.
  4. Forgetting ATR changes. ATR from 2 weeks ago may be very different from current ATR. Use the CURRENT ATR value when sizing each new trade.
  5. Setting SL at 0.5× ATR or less. Almost always gets stopped on noise. Minimum 0.75× ATR for stops to have any breathing room.

BTC 4H chart. Account = $10,000. Risk per trade = 1% = $100.

You spot a bullish setup at $60,000 (support level + reversal candle + volume + RSI bullish divergence). The structural SL would be at $58,500 (below the recent swing low — $1,500 distance, 2.5% from entry).

4H ATR = $1,200. So 1.5× ATR = $1,800.

Comparing:

  • Structural SL at $58,500 = $1,500 distance = 1.25× ATR. Comfortably above the 0.75× ATR minimum and below the 2× ATR threshold. Use it.
  • Notional = $100 / ($1,500/$60,000) = $100 / 0.025 = $4,000.

TPs:

  • TP1 at 2× ATR = $60,000 + $2,400 = $62,400 (1.6:1 R:R)
  • TP2 at 3.5× ATR = $60,000 + $4,200 = $64,200 (2.8:1 R:R)

Two days later, ATR has compressed to $800 (calm regime). You set up another trade. The same math now produces tighter stops, smaller notional adjustments — automatically adapting to the new regime.

blocks.title: Take this with you
blocks.content:
Three rules:

  1. SL = ~1.5× ATR for most active trading. Adapts to asset volatility automatically.
  2. Combine ATR with structural SL. Best is when both align (structural level is also at appropriate ATR distance).
  3. Use current ATR per trade. ATR changes with regime. Pull the current value when sizing each new trade.

You've now covered all 8 indicators in Tier 3. The Tier 3 Final tests integration. Then Tier 4 (Advanced) begins — order flow, Wyckoff, SMC concepts.
